newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stresses its central role in Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stresses its central role in Mideast peace.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday reaffirmed its "central role" in Middle East peace-making, in an apparent polite brush-off to a European Union proposal for a joint initiative.

French officials said on Tuesday that the 15-nation EU had agreed on the move to revive troubled Middle East peace negotiations and that Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok would write to U.S. President Bill Clinton to propose it.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington welcomed the efforts of the Europeans to play a productive role, and wanted to work with them.

"But there's a central point here that has to be raised, and I think it's important to remind everybody about it," Burns told a news briefing. "The United States has the central role in the Middle East peace negotiations."
"The United States will continue to play the central role because that is our historic mission in the Middle East and has been for a quarter century," he added.
Arab states have sometimes sought to involve Europe in peace efforts, but Israel has been leery of any major European role, believing the EU is too sympathetic to the Arab cause.
The United States and Russia are nominally co-sponsors of the peace process started by the 1991 Madrid conference, but in practice Washington has dominated mediation efforts.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held talks on Monday with Clinton to try to break the current impasse but there was no visible sign of a breakthrough.
Two senior Palestinian officials are on their way to Washington to hear the latest U.S. proposals from Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and special envoy Dennis Ross.
The peace process has been deadlocked since Israel broke ground last month on a Jewish housing project in mainly Arab East Jerusalem, enraging Palestinians and sparking often violent street protests.

Burns said Albright on Wednesday engaged in "telephone shuttle diplomacy", calling Saudi Arabian Foreign Minister Saud al-Faisal, Qatari Foreign Minister Hamad bin Jasim, King Hussein of Jordan, Tunisian Foreign Minister Abderrahim Zouari and Sultan Qaboos of Oman.
She also planned to call King Hassan of Morocco, he said.

Burns said the calls were "part of her effort to keep the lines open to the Arab world" but would not confirm that they were related to a recent Arab League call to freeze the normalisation of ties with Israel.
Burns said neither Albright nor Ross had any plans at present to visit the Middle East.
